speaker: Ilya Sutskever
title: Ilya Sutskever – We're moving from the age of scaling to the age of research
question: In frontier AI labs, what structural dynamics drove the shift from pure pre-training scaling back toward fundamental research?
guest: The big breakthrough of pre-training is the realization that this recipe is good. You say, "Hey, if you mix some compute with some data into a neural net of a certain size, you will get results, and you know you'll be better if you just scale the recipe up." Companies love this because it gives you a very low-risk way of investing your resources. It's much harder to invest your resources in research—where you tell researchers to go forth and come up with something—versus getting more data and more compute where you know you'll get something from pre-training. At some point, though, pre-training will run out of data. The data is very clearly finite. So what do you do next? Either you do a different recipe from the one you've done before, or RL, or something else. Now that compute is already very big, is the belief really that if you just 100x the scale, everything would be transformed? It will be different for sure, but I don't think everything would be transformed. So it's back to research again, just with big computers.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The shift was driven mainly by diminishing returns colliding with hard constraints. Through roughly 2020–2023, scaling parameters, data, and compute yielded predictable gains, so labs rationally concentrated resources on engineering larger runs. Several dynamics then eroded that logic.

First, high-quality human text was largely exhausted, so bigger models had less new data to learn from, and each successive generation showed smaller benchmark gains per dollar. Second, costs grew superlinearly: training runs reached billions of dollars and were bottlenecked by chips, power, and data-centre construction timelines, making each scaling bet slower and riskier. Third, competitors converged; with similar architectures and data, scale alone stopped being a differentiator, and efficient entrants like DeepSeek showed that algorithmic cleverness could substitute for brute compute.

Meanwhile, the biggest gains began coming from elsewhere: reasoning models using test-time compute, reinforcement learning on top of pre-training, synthetic data, and agentic scaffolding. That shifted the marginal return toward ideas rather than size. Persistent weaknesses in reliability, long-horizon planning, continual learning, and sample efficiency reinforced the view, voiced by figures like Sutskever, that new research breakthroughs, not just scale, were required.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Frontier AI labs shifted from pure pre-training scaling back to fundamental research when the predictable formula of pairing larger GPU clusters with more internet text hit converging technical and economic walls. Most directly, high-quality human text proved finite while compute kept compounding, breaking balanced scaling laws and yielding diminishing capability gains relative to the soaring capital and energy costs of giant base runs. Post-training reinforcement learning and test-time compute absorbed some surplus hardware, but they also exposed deeper paradigm limits: models excelled on narrow, verifiable benchmarks yet remained sample-inefficient, brittle out of distribution, and unable to learn continually from real-world experience. Meanwhile, competitive dynamics eroded the moat of brute-force scale as standard Transformer recipes diffused across rival and open-weight labs. Left with massive, already-built compute fleets that could no longer buy durable differentiation through scale alone, labs saw their internal incentives invert—redirecting talent and compute away from low-risk scaling execution toward exploratory breakthroughs in continual learning, sample-efficient generalization, world models, and new architectures.

noweb.answer:
Frontier AI labs pivoted from pure pre-training scaling back toward fundamental research when brute-force scaling hit converging data, economic, and capability walls. First, labs largely exhausted the finite supply of high-quality human text, causing marginal capability gains per pre-training FLOP to flatten. Simultaneously, scaling clusters by further orders of magnitude ran into severe capital, energy, and hardware-reliability constraints, turning monolithic training runs into slow, high-risk bets with punishing iteration cycles. At the same time, standard pre-training recipes commoditized across competitors while leaving core deficits—such as brittle out-of-distribution generalization, poor sample efficiency, and the absence of continual learning—unresolved by parameter count alone.

The decisive catalyst was the success of reinforcement learning and test-time compute scaling, which demonstrated that allocating compute to reasoning, search, and verification delivered steeper gains per dollar than simply enlarging base models. Together, diminishing pre-training returns and the emergence of higher-leverage algorithmic axes compelled labs to reorganize around fundamental breakthroughs in post-training, novel architectures, memory, synthetic data generation, and world modeling rather than sheer scale.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Several structural pressures converged. The first was a **data wall**. High-quality human text was close to exhausted, so making a model bigger without more fresh data gave weaker returns. Ilya Sutskever called this "peak data." Very large runs such as GPT-4.5 (the model code-named Orion) cost enormous amounts but improved only modestly.

**Economics** made this worse. Each tenfold increase in compute cost billions, while the gains became harder to see. When every lab followed the same recipe, their models converged and the recipe stopped being an advantage.

The second pressure was a **generalization gap**. Models scored very well on benchmarks but were brittle in real use, which suggested the limit was the method, not scale. Sutskever said in late 2025 that the field was moving from an "age of scaling" back to an "age of research."

Third, the next lever, **reinforcement learning and reasoning**, raised new research problems: reward design, sample efficiency, continual learning and long-horizon agency. More compute alone doesn't solve them.

Finally, **talent and capital** moved toward new research-first labs such as Safe Superintelligence (SSI) and Thinking Machines. Ideas, not just GPUs, became the main way for labs to set themselves apart.

Third, pure next-token prediction exposed a persistent generalization gap: ever-larger base models still struggled with reliable multi-step reasoning, continual learning, and novel problem-solving. Finally, the marginal return on research overtook the marginal return on raw scale. First, high-quality public human text approached exhaustion, causing naive parameter and compute scaling to yield flatter capability gains per dollar. At the same time, frontier training runs became multi-billion-dollar bets constrained by chip supply, power availability, and long feedback cycles, drastically reducing how often labs could iterate on base models alone. Finally, competitive dynamics eroded scale as a durable moat: as pre-training recipes diffused and open-weight models narrowed the gap, raw compute became easier to replicate than novel paradigms. Together, these pressures made fundamental research—into reasoning, sample efficiency, new architectures, and continual or agentic learning—the highest-leverage path to sustained frontier advantage.

Pre-training scaling gave frontier labs a predictable way to improve models. Once the recipe worked, leaders could justify bigger budgets, organize large teams around a shared goal, and compete by securing more chips and data. That made a larger training run easier to fund than a speculative research idea. [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/publications/can-ai-scaling-continue-through-2030)

As runs grew more expensive and high-quality data became harder to find, each additional gain took more resources. Labs were also converging on similar recipes, and larger models still struggled to generalize reliably to unfamiliar tasks. That shifted the competitive advantage toward discovering better ways to train models and use compute, including reinforcement learning and giving models more time to reason at inference. Labs kept scaling, but deciding *what* to scale became a research question again. [Reuters](https://news-static.webullfintech.com/us/news-html/20241111/11771108816438272.html)

noweb.answer:
Pre-training scaling gave frontier labs a predictable way to improve models: spend more on compute, train on more data, and build larger models. That rewarded labs that could raise capital and run enormous training jobs, and it concentrated talent and infrastructure around a shared recipe.

As high-quality training data grew harder to find and each larger run became more expensive, the gains from that recipe became less compelling. Bigger models still struggled with problems such as reliable reasoning and generalization. At the same time, leading labs had accumulated enough compute to test new ideas at meaningful scale. That shifted the competitive advantage toward discovering better training methods, learning from new kinds of feedback, and using compute more effectively at inference time.

models.answer:
For a time, frontier labs had a reliable way to improve models: train a larger one on more data. That predictability favored engineering over open-ended research. A lab racing to release its next model could plan a bigger training run with more confidence than it could count on an algorithmic breakthrough.

As runs grew more expensive, high-quality data became harder to expand, and additional pre-training yielded less predictable gains on the capabilities labs cared about. The cost of a disappointing run rose along with the potential payoff from a better training method. That shifted the balance toward fundamental questions about how models learn and reason, including how to use reinforcement learning and computation at inference time. Pre-training continued to scale, but it became one of several ways a lab could spend its next dollar of compute.
